analysis.one_liner: Rewrites product injury lawsuits under one federal standard, shielding manufacturers and sellers from most punitive damages.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors and never got a hearing or vote; it died in House subcommittees before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced state product-liability laws with one uniform federal rule for anyone harmed by a defective product. It would have shortened the deadline to sue to two years, made it much harder to win punitive damages, barred punitive damages entirely against makers of FDA-approved drugs and FAA-certified aircraft, reduced jury awards for injured workers by their workers' compensation benefits, and protected retail sellers from most lawsuits. Its stated purpose was uniformity and lower costs for businesses; its effect would have been fewer and smaller recoveries for people hurt by defective products.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and sellers of consumer and industrial products, especially drug, medical device, and aircraft makers, and the liability insurers who pay their claims. They would face fewer lawsuits, shorter exposure periods, no punitive damages for approved drugs and certified aircraft, and smaller jury awards — which means lower legal and insurance costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Product makers, drug and aircraft companies, insurers

how_it_helps.text: Bars punitive damages against manufacturers of FDA-approved drugs and medical devices and FAA-certified aircraft, unless the company defrauded or bribed the agency during approval [S2][S3].

Raises the proof standard for punitive damages to 'clear and convincing evidence' of 'conscious, flagrant indifference' to safety, and says ordinary carelessness in choosing a design or warning does not qualify [S2][S3].
Bars most lawsuits filed more than two years after the injury was or should have been discovered, and bars claims about used-in-business capital goods more than 25 years after delivery [S2][S3].
Reduces any damages award for an injured worker by the workers' compensation benefits the worker is or would be entitled to receive [S2][S3].
Makes each defendant pay only its own share of pain-and-suffering damages, so an injured person bears the loss when another defendant cannot pay [S2][S3].

Shields retail sellers and distributors from liability unless they were negligent or broke an express warranty, and lets defendants demand that punitive damages be decided in a separate proceeding [S2][S3].
Gives defendants a complete defense if the injured person was intoxicated and more than 50 percent responsible for the accident [S2][S3].
Pressures quick settlement through mandatory settlement offers and fee-shifting, and sanctions for refusing alternative dispute resolution [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed by defective products. They would have less time to file, a far higher bar for punitive damages, reduced awards offset by workers' compensation, and no recovery of full pain-and-suffering damages when one responsible party cannot pay. The bill would also override state laws that currently give those people stronger remedies.

drawbacks.text: The punitive-damages bar for FDA-approved drugs and FAA-certified aircraft would leave families of people harmed by approved products with no punitive remedy even where a company's behavior was reckless, as long as it had not defrauded the regulator [S2][S3].
The two-year filing deadline could extinguish claims for latent injuries, such as toxic exposures, discovered later [S2][S3].

Making liability for pain-and-suffering several rather than joint shifts uncompensated losses to injured people when a defendant is bankrupt or uninsured, instead of letting manufacturers spread the cost of defects through prices and insurance [S3].

The supporters' strongest counterargument: inconsistent state liability rules raised costs and insurance premiums for manufacturers and made it hard to defend against forum shopping, and a uniform rule could lower prices. But the bill's specific limits go well beyond uniformity, cutting back on remedies many states had deliberately strengthened [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The uniformity argument has some real force — a company selling in 50 states faced 50 sets of liability rules. But the substance of this bill is one-sided: nearly every operative provision lowers a manufacturer's exposure, and none raises it. The cost falls on precisely the people the civil justice system exists to compensate — those hurt by defective drugs, aircraft, machinery, and consumer goods. The few claimant-friendly features (blocking employer liens on recoveries, preserving environmental suits) do not offset the core liability rollbacks.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House subcommittees after being referred in the summer of 1991 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bob McEwen introduced the bill on July 29, 1991, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees [S1][S5].
It was sent to the Economic and Commercial Law subcommittee on August 13, 1991, and to the Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness subcommittee on August 30, 1991 [S5].
No further action was ever recorded, and the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, without a vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People injured by defective products are better off: the state liability rules the bill would have preempted remain in force. Manufacturers, drug and aircraft companies, and insurers did not gain the liability protections they sought, and the plaintiffs' bar kept its practice.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern on the merits ever formed.

industries.note: The bill would have shortened their legal exposure, protected non-manufacturer sellers, and limited their share of pain-and-suffering awards. The savings come from amounts that would otherwise have gone to people hurt by defective products.

Punitive damages would be barred for any FDA-approved drug or device, with an exception only for companies that defrauded or bribed the agency. FDA approval would become a near-complete shield, at the expense of patients harmed by approved products.

Punitive damages would be barred for FAA-certified aircraft when the manufacturer met continuing airworthiness duties. Passengers and workers injured in crashes involving certified designs would lose that remedy.

Shorter deadlines, harder punitive standards, workers' compensation offsets, and several liability all shrink payouts, cutting insurers' claim costs while injured people absorb more of their own losses.

Fewer viable claims, fee-shifting that penalizes rejecting low settlement offers, and mandatory alternate dispute resolution would shrink this industry's case volume. Its interest here runs with that of injured clients.
